senses.gloss:
Drāviḍa
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in the dharmaśāstra literature in several senses. ‘Drāviḍa’ is the name of a caste classed among the शूद्रस्. Persons of this caste are supposed to have sprung from the kṣattriyas who had not undergone the Vedic sacraments like उपनयन.
The ब्राह्मणस् of India have been divided into two groups: pañca-द्राविड and pañca-gauḍa. The karṇāṭas, the tailaṅgas, the gurjaris, the mahārāṣṭrians and the drāviḍas belong to the former group. Among these, the drāviḍas are also one.
Among the three well-known styles of temple architecture, द्राविड is also one, the other two being नागर and वेसर. The द्राविड style is in the form of truncated pyramids and is more common in the region to the south of the river Kṛṣṇā.

Draviḍians
------------------------------------------
The question of the ancient people of India, whether they were the original inhabitants or immigrants, has always received great attention at the hands of historians, indologists, anthropologists and philologists. Several hypotheses and theories have been advanced over the last two centuries though no particular school of thought has been universally acclaimed or even gained a majority of adherents.
One such vexatious question is that of the आर्यन्स् and the द्रविडिअन्स्. If some say that the द्रविडिअन्स् were the original inhabitants of India, driven to the southern peninsula by the invading आर्यन्स्, there are others who declare that they too were immigrants who came from the Mediterranean region much earlier than the आर्यन्स्.
However, there is also another view that the हरप्प-मोहेन्जो दारो culture is the advanced stage of Vedic culture—and hence has nothing to do with the so-called Draviḍian culture—and that the Draviḍian languages like Tamil, Telugu and Kannada are gradual evolutions from the प्राकृत् and Paiśācī languages which themselves were derivatives of the सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे.
There has been so much of racial commingling and complicated evolutions of languages over the millennia that no single theory can be accepted as unquestioningly authentic.
Since अगस्त्य, the great Vedic sage, had been universally acclaimed as the originator of the religion, language and culture of South India (which later spread to the South East Asian countries also), suffice it to say that the Āryan-Draviḍian divide is more a conjecture than a well-established fact.
See also AGASTYA and ĀRYANS.

draṣṭā
(‘the seer’)
------------------------------------------
According to the various works on the Vedānta system of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्, each one of us is actually the आत्मन्, the सोउल्, whose real nature is ‘sat-cit-आनन्द’ (existence, knowledge and bliss). This आत्मन् has become involved and identified with the body-मिन्द् complex due to prim-eval इग्नोरन्चे which, however, can be annihilated by ज्ञान or knowledge. The process of discrimination between the dṛk or द्रष्टा (the seer, the witness or the subject) and the दृश्य (the seen, the object) will help in ultimately isolating the आत्मन् from the body, the senses and the मिन्द्.
For instance, an external object is दृश्य and the eye is the dṛk. Again, the eye becomes the दृश्य for the मिन्द् which is now dṛk. However, even this मिन्द् becomes the दृश्य for the आत्मन्, the conscious Self. There is none who is the dṛk for the आत्मन्. Hence the आत्मन् is the ultimate dṛk or द्रष्टा. The द्रष्टा who is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् continues to remain so eventhough there may be nothing to become दृश्य for him. For instance, in pitch darkness, in an empty room, though the eye is ‘seeing,’ there is nothing to be ‘seen.’ Similarly, the द्रष्टा, the आत्मन् as the ultimate witness is always the conscious subject or the seer and there is no loss of his चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् irrespective of the existence or non-existence of objects to be comprehended by him.

dravya
(‘substance’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘dravya’ has been used widely in several senses, including the technical ones in some systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्. The general senses are: wealth, an object or substance, an auspicious one, an ointment, intoxicating liquid, medicine and bronze.
In the न्याय system of गौतम, ‘dravya’ is one of the seven padārthas or fundamental substances in the universe. This ‘dravya’ is of nine types: the five bhūtas or elements, kāla (time), dik (quarters or directions), आत्मन् (the individual सोउल्) and मनस् (mind).
In the द्वैत Vedānta system, it comprises 20 items such as परमात्मन् (God), लक्ष्मी (The Divine consort of God), jīvātman (the individual सोउल्), प्रकृति (nature), the three guṇas like सत्त्व, बुद्धि (intellect), indriya (senses), अविद्या (ignorance) and so on.
On the other hand, the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta recognises only six items under द्रव्य. They are: प्रकृति (nature), kāla (time), śuddha or pure सत्त्व, धर्म-भूत-ज्ञान (knowledge as an attribute of the जीव), जीव (individual सोउल्) and ईश्वर (god).
The substances like fuel-sticks of अश्वत्थ (Ficus religiosa), sesamum seeds, pudding of milk, ghee, sweetmeats, coconuts, jaggery, honey and certain fruits—are also called ‘dravya’ or ‘homadravya’ and are used in homas or sacrifices.
In the आयुर्वेद (health science) seven dravyas like vāta (wind), pitta (bile), śleṣma (phlegm), tvak (skin) and māṁsa (flesh) are recognised as comprising the physical body.

dravyayajña
(‘sacrifice with wealth’)
------------------------------------------
Yajña or the system of sacrifices is an ancient institution. According to the Hindu scriptures like the Bhagavadgītā (3.10) it was created by प्रजापति (father of च्रेअतिओन्) himself in the beginning as a link between the gods in हेअवेन् and the human beings here. The human beings have to satiate the gods like इन्द्र through यज्ञ and the latter in return bestow rains and grant other things needed by the human beings.
Though Śrī कृष्ण has accepted this basic system, he has expanded its scope considerably in the Bhagavadgītā (4.25-33). It is in this connection that he has used the word ‘dravyayajña’ (4.28). It is interpreted as giving money or things to worthy and deserving persons at the appropriate time and place, and, in an appropriate manner.
The most important act in a यज्ञ is sacrificing the individual good for social or universal good. In whichever act, such a spirit is seen, that itself is elevated to the level of a यज्ञ.
